title: Addresses and Names: IP and DNS
summary: Every computer on the Internet needs an address number, just like every house needs a street address. But numbers are hard to remember, so clever people built a giant shared phone book called DNS that turns names like example.com into numbers. And when the Internet started running out of numbers, engineers invented a new kind of address with more than enough for every grain of sand on Earth!

sections.heading: Every Door Needs a Number
paragraphs: In Part 7 we rode along with a packet as routers passed it from hop to hop. Every one of those routers made its choice by reading a single thing: the destination address in the packet's header. Without addresses, routers would be like postal workers holding a pile of blank envelopes. So where do these addresses come from, and what do they look like?

The Internet's addresses are called IP addresses, because they belong to the Internet Protocol. The classic kind, used since the early 1980s, is IPv4, version 4 of the protocol. An IPv4 address is a number 32 bits long. Long strings of 1s and 0s are hard for people to read, so we usually split the 32 bits into four groups of 8 bits, turn each group into an ordinary number from 0 to 255, and put dots between them. An example looks like this: 192.0.2.1.

That particular address is special. Engineers set aside the block starting 192.0.2 just for examples in books and documents, so that nobody accidentally sends real traffic to a real person's computer by copying an example. You will never find a real website living there, which makes it perfect for a story like this one.

An IP address works a lot like a postal address, which runs from big to small: country, city, street, house. The first part of an IP address usually identifies a network, such as a university or an Internet provider, and the last part identifies one particular device on that network. Routers far away only need to look at the first part to send a packet in the right direction, just as a sorting office in another country only needs to read the country name. When the packet gets close, routers look at the rest.

Your home is a good example of how this works in practice. Your Internet provider usually gives your home router one public IP address that the rest of the world can see. Inside your house, the router hands out private addresses, often starting with 192.168, to your laptop, tablet, games console and smart speaker. When those devices go online, the router swaps their private address for the public one on the way out, and keeps careful notes so it can deliver the replies to the right device. This trick is called network address translation, or NAT. It means a whole family, or even a whole office, can share one public address, a bit like an apartment block with one street number and a front desk that sorts the mail for each flat.

How does a new phone or laptop get its private address in the first place? Nobody types it in. When a device joins a Wi-Fi network, it shouts a short message that means roughly, 'Hello, I am new here, can somebody give me an address?' The router answers with a free address, plus a few other useful details, such as which way leads out to the Internet and which server to ask about names. This automatic system is called DHCP, and it lends each address for a limited time, a bit like a library book, so that addresses from devices that have left can be reused. That is why your tablet's address at home might change from one week to the next, and why it gets a completely different one when you connect at a friend's house.

Numbers are perfect for routers. But imagine if, to visit a website or send an email, you had to remember a string of numbers for every place you wanted to go. People are much better with names. The story of how the Internet learned to use names begins with a single, ever-growing list, and a woman whose team kept it.

sections.heading: One List for the Whole Network
paragraphs: In the early days of the ARPANET, the network was small enough for everyone to know everyone else. Computers had short names, and somebody needed to keep track of which name belonged to which address. That job went to the Network Information Center, or NIC, at SRI, the same research institute in California that had received the very first ARPANET message in 1969.

The NIC was run by Elizabeth Feinler, known to her colleagues as Jake. She had trained as a chemist and had worked on huge reference books before joining SRI in 1960, where in 1972 she joined Douglas Engelbart's research centre. That background in organising information turned out to be exactly what the young network needed. From 1972 until 1989, Feinler's group managed the registry of host names for the network. They also published directories of the people and machines on the ARPANET, a kind of early 'white pages' and 'yellow pages' for the network, and they ran one of the first servers that could answer questions about who owned a name, a service called WHOIS.

The heart of the naming system was a single text file, usually called HOSTS.TXT. Each line paired a computer's name with its address. Whenever a new computer joined the network, or an old one changed its address, the people running it contacted the NIC, the NIC updated the master file, and every computer on the network was expected to download a fresh copy now and then. Today's computers still contain a small leftover of this idea, a file simply called 'hosts', which you can find hidden inside the system folders of Windows, macOS and Linux.

For a network of a few dozen, or even a few hundred, computers, one shared list worked well. But in the early 1980s, things were changing fast. Universities and companies were plugging in whole local networks full of workstations, and the number of machines was shooting up. Every new computer meant another change to the file, and every change meant thousands of copies around the network slowly going out of date. The list was getting too big, updated too often, and sent around too much. It was like trying to run the phone book for an entire country from one office, by posting a new printed copy to every home whenever anyone moved house.

In a technical document in November 1983, the problem was described plainly: the size of the table, and especially how often it had to be updated, were 'near the limit of manageability'. Something completely new was needed.

sections.heading: Paul Mockapetris Builds a Phone Book That Shares the Work
paragraphs: The person who designed that something new was Paul Mockapetris, a young computer scientist at the University of Southern California's Information Sciences Institute (ISI) in Marina del Rey, near Los Angeles. ISI was a busy hub of Internet work. Jon Postel, who edited the RFCs and kept track of the Internet's numbers, worked there too, and the two of them, together with others in the community, had been discussing how to replace the overloaded host table. In 1983 Mockapetris wrote up his design in two documents, RFC 882 and RFC 883. He called it the Domain Name System, or DNS.

His key idea was to stop keeping one giant list in one place. Instead, the job would be shared out among thousands of computers, each responsible for its own small piece. The names themselves would be arranged like a family tree, or like a set of folders inside folders.

At the very top of the tree is the root, which has no name at all. Just below the root sit the top-level domains, such as com, org and uk. Below each of those come the names that organisations choose, such as example under com. And below those, an organisation can create as many more names as it likes for its own computers, such as www or mail. When we write a full name, we read it from the most specific part on the left to the most general on the right, with dots in between: www.example.com means 'the computer called www, inside example, inside com, inside the root'.

The really clever part is called delegation. The people who run the root do not need to know about every name. They only need to know who is in charge of each top-level domain. The people running com only need to know who is in charge of each name like example. And the people running example decide everything underneath it themselves. If a school wants to add a new computer called library, it does not need to ask anyone else in the world. It just updates its own little part of the tree.

This made DNS like a phone book that writes itself. No single office has to handle every change, and no single list has to be copied to every computer. Instead, when a computer needs an address, it asks around, starting from the top of the tree and working down, until it finds the server that knows the answer.

To make this fast, DNS also uses caching, which means remembering answers for a while. Each answer comes with a 'time to live' saying how long it can be trusted, perhaps a few minutes, perhaps a day. Once your Internet provider's DNS server has looked up a popular name, it can answer the next thousand people who ask straight from memory. DNS was first described in 1983 and was being put into use from 1984, and over the following years it replaced HOSTS.TXT completely. It later became one of the Internet's original official standards, and it is still working away, billions of times a day, every time you open a website, send an email or start an online game.

sections.heading: Dot-Com, Dot-Org, Dot-Everything
paragraphs: Once there was a tree, someone had to decide what the first branches should be. In October 1984, Jon Postel and his colleague Joyce Reynolds published RFC 920, which listed the first general top-level domains. There was gov for government, edu for education, com for commercial businesses, mil for the military and org for other organisations. A temporary domain called arpa was kept for the old ARPANET names. Elizabeth Feinler's group at the NIC also played a big part in shaping this scheme, and the net domain, meant for network organisations, soon joined the list.

RFC 920 also planned for countries. Each country could have its own two-letter top-level domain, based on an international list of country codes. At the time the document was written, no country domains existed yet. The first ones arrived in 1985: us for the United States, uk for the United Kingdom and il for Israel. Many more followed. China's cn arrived in the early 1990s, and today there are well over 300 country-code domains, including versions written in non-Latin scripts such as Chinese, Arabic and Cyrillic.

Some small countries have found that their two letters are worth a lot. The Pacific island nation of Tuvalu has the code tv, which is popular with television and video companies, and the money from selling those names has become an important source of income for the country.

The very first name registered in com was symbolics.com, on 15 March 1985. It belonged to Symbolics, a company in Massachusetts that made powerful computers designed for artificial-intelligence research, called Lisp machines. Back then, a com name was free to register and hardly anyone wanted one. Only a handful of companies registered com names during all of 1985. Symbolics itself later faded away, but its domain lives on as a piece of Internet history, and in 2009 it was bought by a domain investment company that keeps it as a kind of online museum page.

Compare that slow start with today. There are now hundreds of millions of registered domain names, with com still by far the most popular. Since the 2010s, the list of top-level domains has also grown to include more than a thousand new endings, from app and blog to city names and brand names. Each one is just another branch at the top of Mockapetris's tree.

sections.heading: Jon Postel, Keeper of the Numbers
paragraphs: Names and numbers only work if they are unique. If two computers had the same address, routers would not know which one to deliver to, like two houses on the same street with the same number. So somebody has to hand out the numbers and keep the master records. For most of the Internet's first thirty years, that somebody was largely one man: Jon Postel.

Postel had been a graduate student in Leonard Kleinrock's lab at UCLA, where the first ARPANET node was installed, and he earned his doctorate there in 1974. When Steve Crocker started the Request for Comments series in 1969, Postel soon became its editor, a job he held for almost three decades. He read, polished and published the documents that described how the Internet worked, including key ones about IP, TCP, email and DNS. He was famous for a simple piece of advice for anyone writing network software, often called the robustness principle: be careful in what you send, but generous in what you accept from others.

Postel also volunteered to keep track of the numbers that the Internet's rules needed, such as which address blocks belonged to which networks and which port numbers belonged to which services. At first he did it by hand. Friends jokingly called him the 'numbers czar'. This job grew into the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, or IANA. With his long beard and relaxed style, Postel did not look like a powerful official, but for years a surprising amount of the Internet's smooth running depended on his careful record-keeping at ISI.

As the Internet became a worldwide public network in the 1990s, many people felt that such an important job should not rest with one person and one small government-funded office. After long discussions involving the United States government, businesses, engineers and other countries, a new organisation was created in 1998: the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, or ICANN. It is a non-profit organisation based in California, and its policies are shaped by a wide mix of people, including businesses, governments, technical experts and ordinary Internet users. It took over the IANA functions, including looking after the root of the DNS tree and the master pool of IP addresses.

Sadly, Postel did not see ICANN grow up. He died on 16 October 1998, aged 55, just as the new organisation was being set up. The next day Vint Cerf wrote a memorial, published as RFC 2468, called 'I Remember IANA', describing him as the first of the Internet's giants to depart. The Internet Society later created the Postel Service Award in his honour.

Today, IANA does not hand out addresses to people directly. It passes big blocks of addresses to five regional Internet registries, each looking after one part of the world: ARIN for North America, RIPE NCC for Europe, the Middle East and parts of Central Asia, APNIC for Asia and the Pacific, LACNIC for Latin America and the Caribbean, and AFRINIC for Africa. They pass smaller blocks to Internet providers, who in turn give addresses to homes, schools and businesses. In 2016 the United States government formally ended its special oversight role, leaving the IANA functions in the hands of the global community through ICANN.

sections.heading: Running Out of Numbers
paragraphs: When the designers of IPv4 chose 32-bit addresses in the 1970s, it seemed like an enormous number. Thirty-two bits allows 2 multiplied by itself 32 times, which comes to 4,294,967,296 addresses, about 4.3 billion. At the time, the whole network had only a few hundred computers. Who could ever need four billion?

In fact, the original plan was even more limited. The first 8 bits of an address were used to name the network, and the other 24 bits named the computer inside it. That allowed only 256 networks, which seemed plenty when there were only a few big research networks. When local networks started appearing everywhere in the 1980s, engineers changed the rules, first by creating different 'classes' of address blocks of different sizes, and later, in 1993, by allowing blocks of almost any size. Even so, some early organisations had been given gigantic blocks of about 16.7 million addresses each, far more than they would ever use.

By the 1990s it was clear that the world was going to want far more than 4.3 billion addresses. Today there are more people on Earth than that, and many of them own a phone, a laptop and other connected gadgets. Tricks like NAT, which lets many devices share one public address, bought a lot of time. But the pool of free addresses kept shrinking.

The moment finally came in early 2011. On 3 February 2011, IANA handed out its last five large blocks of IPv4 addresses, one to each of the five regional registries. The central pool of free IPv4 addresses was empty. The regional registries ran out of their own normal supplies over the following years, and today IPv4 addresses are often bought and sold between organisations, sometimes for a noticeable price per address.

The long-term answer had been prepared years earlier: IPv6, version 6 of the Internet Protocol. (Version 5 had been used for an experimental project, so the number was skipped.) The main IPv6 specification first appeared in the 1990s and was finalised as a full Internet Standard in 2017. Its addresses are 128 bits long instead of 32. That gives about 340 undecillion possible addresses, or 3.4 times 10 to the power 38, a 34 followed by 37 zeros. It is a number so large that it is hard to picture; every person alive could have many trillions of trillions of addresses each.

IPv6 addresses look different too. They are written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits, which use the numbers 0 to 9 and the letters a to f, separated by colons. Long runs of zeros can be shortened with a double colon, so an example address, from a block reserved for documentation, can be written as 2001:db8::1. Moving the whole Internet to IPv6 has been slow, because IPv4 and IPv6 cannot talk to each other directly, and every network, router, computer and app needs to support both during the long changeover. But the shift is well under way: a large and growing share of Internet users now reach big websites over IPv6, often without ever knowing it, and in some countries it is already the majority.

sections.heading: What Happens When You Type a Name
paragraphs: Let us put everything together. Imagine you type www.example.org into your browser and press Enter. What happens in the next fraction of a second?

Step one: your browser checks its own memory. If you visited the site a few minutes ago, it may already know the address. If not, it asks your computer's operating system, which keeps its own small memory of recent answers and also glances at that old-fashioned hosts file.

Step two: if your computer does not know, it sends a short question to a DNS server called a recursive resolver. Usually this is run by your Internet provider, though some people choose a public resolver run by another organisation. The resolver's job is to do the detective work for you. If it has answered the same question recently for someone else, it replies immediately from its cache.

Step three: if the resolver does not know either, it starts at the top of the tree. It asks one of the root servers, 'Where can I find www.example.org?' The root server does not know the full answer, but it knows who is in charge of org, and it replies with the addresses of the org servers. There are only 13 named root server identities, lettered A to M and run by twelve different organisations, but thanks to a technique that lets many machines share one address, copies of them are running at well over a thousand places around the world.
Step four: the resolver asks an org server. The org server does not know about www either, but it knows which name servers are in charge of example.org, so it passes on their addresses.

Step five: the resolver asks one of example.org's own name servers, which is called the authoritative server because it holds the official records for that name. This server finally gives the real answer: the IP address for www.example.org.

Step six: the resolver sends the answer back to your computer and remembers it for as long as its time to live allows. Your browser now has a number. It can open a TCP connection to that address with the three-way handshake you met in Part 7, ask for the web page, and receive it as a stream of packets. All of these DNS questions and answers usually take only a few tens of milliseconds, and often much less when the answer is already cached nearby.

So every time you visit a website, you are using two inventions from the early 1980s working together: IP addresses that let routers deliver packets, and DNS names that let humans find those addresses without memorising numbers. In the mid-1980s, though, the people using these systems were still mostly scientists, engineers, university researchers and the military. Ordinary families had never heard of TCP/IP or dot-com. That was about to change.

deepDive: DNS is one of the most successful distributed databases ever built, but it was designed in a gentler era and has had to be strengthened. Early DNS trusted any answer that looked right, so attackers could try to slip in fake answers, a trick called cache poisoning. In 2008 the researcher Dan Kaminsky showed that this was much easier than people had assumed, and software makers around the world rushed out coordinated fixes. A longer-term defence, DNSSEC, adds digital signatures so that resolvers can check that an answer really came from the right owner; the root zone was signed in 2010, although many domains still do not use it. Another concern is privacy: traditional DNS questions travel unencrypted, so anyone along the path can see which sites you look up. Newer methods such as DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS wrap the questions in encryption, which protects users but has also caused debate, because it can bypass network filters used by schools, parents or governments. The 13-letter limit on root server identities comes from an old rule that a DNS answer should fit in a 512-byte UDP packet; techniques called anycast let each letter be served from hundreds of locations, which also makes the root very hard to knock over with floods of traffic. Historians also discuss how much power ICANN really has. It controls what goes into the root zone, which means it can approve new top-level domains such as the more than 1,000 added after 2012, but it does not control the content of websites or the routing of packets. The IPv4 shortage has created a market where address blocks are traded, while IPv6 adoption varies widely from country to country. Some engineers argue that IPv4 and NAT will linger for decades, while others note that mobile networks, which need vast numbers of addresses, have pushed IPv6 forward fastest.
funFact: The DNS root is served by only 13 named server identities, lettered A to M, yet copies of them run at well over a thousand locations around the world.
